text:
Heraclitus walks through the evening

of Ephesus. Evening has left him,

without his will deciding it,

on the bank of a silent river

whose destiny and whose name he does not know.

There is a stone Janus and some poplars.

He looks at himself in the fugitive mirror

and discovers and fashions the sentence

that the generations of men

will not let fall. His voice declares:

No one steps twice into the waters

of the same river. He stops. He feels,

with the amazement of a sacred horror,

that he too is a river and a flight.

He wants to recover that morning

and his night and the eve before. He cannot.

He repeats the sentence. He sees it printed

in future and clear characters

on one of Burnet’s pages.

Heraclitus does not know Greek. Janus,

god of gates, is a Latin god.

Heraclitus has no yesterday or now.

He is a mere artifice dreamed

by a gray man on the banks of the Red Cedar,

a man who interweaves hendecasyllables

so as not to think so much of Buenos Aires

and of beloved faces. One is missing.

translation.title: Heraclitus
translation.editorial_note: The poem’s anachronisms are kept explicit: the philosopher is a literary artifice invented by Borges, whose river is also exile and bereavement.
